- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.  
- If sentiment turns negative (≤0.4) after a spike, model often overshoots downward; cap forecast at 5–10% below peak if sentiment drops sharply.  
- Model frequently overreacts to recent price spikes (especially >70) by forecasting further upward; apply a “cool-down” bias: subtract 3–8% from forecast if recent 3-day high is >72.  
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.2–0.6), model often fails to capture mean reversion; if 3–5 consecutive days show downward trend, forecast should trend downward by 1–3% per day.  
- If model forecast is >75 and sentiment is low, reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid overestimating “bullish” momentum.  
- If true outcome is consistently below model (especially in 3–5 consecutive days), apply a “reversion bias”: forecast should be adjusted downward by 1–3% per day if sentiment remains flat or negative.  
- Model tends to ignore sentiment shifts in early horizon (e.g., 1–3 days ahead); if sentiment changes sharply within 3 days, adjust forecast to reflect sentiment shift within 1–2 days.
